extracted.intended_audience: students of English literature (undergraduate/MA); readers learning archetypal criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for interpreting literary texts using Northrop Frye's archetypal / mythical approach, including methods (inductive/deductive), the role of structural and historical criticism, myth phases, rhythm/pattern, and comic vs tragic vision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archetypal criticism: interpret in light of cultural patterns (myths and rituals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Archetypal approach is the interpretation of a text in the light of cultural patterns involved in it, and these cultural patterns are based on the myths and rituals of a race or nation or social group. Myths and rituals are explored in a text for discovery of meaning and message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for recurring mythological patterns and rituals in a work; draw on authorities like Frazer (The Golden Bough) and Jung (collective unconscious) to relate images/symbols to shared cultural/mythic material. Example: T.S. Eliot's The Waste Land uses mythical patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningful vs meaningless criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two types of literary criticism: a significant and meaningful criticism, and a meaningless criticism. A meaningless criticism will not help a reader in developing a systematic structure of knowledge about a work of literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for criticism that builds systematic, organized knowledge about a work rather than merely giving background or superficial commentary; meaningful criticism synthesizes methods and reveals deeper patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synthesis of structural (formalistic) and historical criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Structural criticism confines itself to the text and helps understand pattern; historical criticism provides background information that explains how the pattern evolved. What readers require is a synthesis of structural criticism and historical criticism. Archetypal criticism is a synthesis of both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine close textual analysis (form, pattern, images) with historical/contextual research (origins of symbols, social/cultural milieu) rather than privileging one approach alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary criticism as a systematic/scientific discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary criticism today has become systematic in its analysis and therefore it could be considered as a science. Frye uses two methods: structural criticism and historical criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply organized methods (explicit inductive and deductive procedures) and scholarly organization when analyzing texts; treat criticism as a structured inquiry that can be taught and learned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive method (structural criticism): move from particulars to general truths
rubrics_metrics.description: Under structural criticism the critic proceeds inductively: from particular truths in a work he draws forth general truths. Example: from Othello's jealousy (particular) a reader learns the general truth that jealousy is always destructive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with concrete textual particulars—events, images, character actions—and infer broader thematic or mythic patterns that those particulars exemplify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivity of the critic and 'discovering' unconscious elements
rubrics_metrics.description: An author cannot intrude into his text and express his personal emotions and comments. He should maintain absolute objectivity. A critic studies a work and finds out whether an author is free from textual interference. At times the author himself may be unconscious of the myths, symbols etc., which he has exploited in his works, and the critic 'discovers' such things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain critical objectivity; analyze the text for latent symbols/myths that may be unconscious on the author's part rather than reading merely authorial intention or biography into every feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical criticism (inductive): relate texts to social and cultural causes; identify archetypal sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Under historical criticism a critic interprets the birth of a text as an outcome of social and cultural demands of a society in a particular period. The historical critic discovers common symbols and images used by different writers and resolves that there must be a common source from which writers have derived their symbols, images and myths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace symbols (e.g., the sea) across writers and periods to establish archetypal status; situate genres in historical origins (e.g., drama's origin in Greek religion). Use social/cultural milieu as explanatory cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective unconscious / racial memory: trace primitive myth/ritual origins
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols, myths and rituals in literature have their origin in primitive myths, rituals, folklore and cultures that lie buried in the 'collective unconscious' or 'racial memory' of a people; because a writer is part of a race, such unconscious material appears in his works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting symbols, consider anthropological and Jungian roots—seek primitive/folk sources and ritual parallels that might explain recurring motifs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdisciplinary, specialized scholarly organization in archetypal criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Archetypal criticism is an all-inclusive term involving many specialists: an editor to clean up the text; a rhetorician to analyze narrative pace; a philologist to scrutinize word choice; a literary social historian to study evolution of myths and rituals; a literary anthropologist to trace sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use or emulate interdisciplinary expertise: combine editorial, rhetorical, philological, historical and anthropological methods to construct a full archetypal reading (example: tracing Hamlet to Saxo and nature myths).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive method: move from general myth to particular textual meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the deductive method the critic proceeds from the general truth (a myth) to the particular truth (why a character behaves so) and establishes the meaning of a work from a myth down to text-level specifics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with large mythic patterns (e.g., resurrection, descent) or genre archetypes and apply them to explain specific plot events, character motives, and symbolic details in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm in literature: narrative tempo and recurrence
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhythm is an essential characteristic of music and in literature rhythm means the narrative; it presents all events and episodes as a sequence and hastens action. In literature both rhythm and pattern are recurrence of images, forms and words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze the narrative pacing, sequence of events, and recurrence of motifs as 'rhythm'—relate these to natural/ritual cycles (seasons, rites) to reveal meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern in literature: verbal structure and recurrence from epiphanic moments
rubrics_metrics.description: Pattern in literature signifies its verbal structure and conveys meaning. Patterns are derived from a writer’s 'epiphanic moments'—proverbs, riddles, commandments and etiological folktales that feed the work's narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify recurring verbal structures and stock forms (proverbs, folktales) as manifestations of pattern; explicate how these patterns encode mythic or archetypal meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Four Phases of the Myth and their genre correspondences
rubrics_metrics.description: Frye classifies myths into four categories: (1) dawn/spring/birth phase — archetypes of romance and rhapsodic poetry; (2) zenith/summer/marriage/triumph — archetypes of comedy, pastoral, idyll; (3) sunset/autumn/death — archetypes of tragedy and elegy; (4) darkness/winter/desolation — archetypes of satire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify a work's dominant mythic phase to connect it to corresponding genres and subordinate character types (e.g., father/mother in birth myths; traitor/siren in death myths). Use the fourfold schema to map tone and trajectory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quest-myth as foundational and genre-forming
rubrics_metrics.description: The quest-myth, in which the hero goes in quest of a truth or something else, was supposed to have developed from the four types of myths; Frye argues almost all genres in every literature have been evolved from the quest-myth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting genres and narratives, look for quest structures (search, trials, return) and treat them as a possible master-pattern underlying genres and motifs (example: Messiah/Holy Grail parallels in The Waste Land).

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious archetypes treated as human characters; focus on conceivability and epiphany
rubrics_metrics.description: A literary critic considers God as an archetype of man who is portrayed as a hero in a work. Criticism deals with conceivability rather than scientific actuality; both religion and literary criticism function on conceivability and employ epiphany as revelation originating from the subconscious/dreams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat religious figures and motifs as narrative/archetypal elements subject to literary analysis; emphasize internal conceivability, symbolic epiphany, and psychological dynamics rather than empirical truth-claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic vs tragic vision schema across five 'worlds' to interpret tone and imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Frye outlines comic and tragic visions in five 'worlds' (human, animal, vegetable, mineral, unformed). Each world yields characteristic archetypal images: e.g., comic human = community, friendship, marriage; tragic human = tyranny, isolation; comic animal = flock/pastoral; tragic animal = beasts/predators; comic vegetable = garden/tree of life; tragic vegetable = sinister forest; comic mineral = luminous city/temple; tragic mineral = deserts/ruins; comic unformed = fourfold river; tragic unformed = sea/flood/monster.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether a text predominantly enacts the comic or tragic vision and use the five-world typology to interpret recurring images and their tonal implications (example: Yeats' 'Sailing to Byzantium' as comic vision imagery).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of antithesis (waking/dreaming, light/dark) to locate epiphany
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a cycle of waking and dreaming and a cycle of light and darkness in human life and nature; these antithetic factors bring about epiphany in a person. In the day man develops fear and frustration; in the dark his libido awakens and he resolves to achieve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to oppositions (day/night, light/dark, waking/dreaming) in the text as structural devices that create moments of revelation or epiphany and help explain symbolic dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complementarity and necessity of inductive and deductive methods
rubrics_metrics.description: In mythical criticism both the inductive method and the deductive method are effective tools and neither can be dispensed with. If one method explains a text based on the derivation of a general truth from the particular, the other method does it the other way round.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply both bottom-up (particular→general) and top-down (general→particular) reasoning in interpretation; use them as complementary moves to achieve a fuller archetypal reading.
